Cochrane review (25 RCTs, 3780 participants) found no difference between single-visit and multiple-visit RCT for radiological failure, tooth extraction, swelling, or fistula formation, though single-visit patients reported more first-week pain and analgesic use [[PMID:27905673]]. This review did not analyse cracked teeth as a subgroup, so it cannot be used to stratify prognosis by crack extent — it only supports the general principle that visit number is not a decisive prognostic variable when RCT is undertaken. The Del Fabbro et al. Cochrane review of surgical vs. non-surgical retreatment (20 RCTs) similarly found no clear superiority of either approach for periapical healing and no cracked-tooth subgroup analysis [[PMID:27759881]].

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

Karaoğlan et al. randomised 100 single-rooted teeth with periapical lesions to single- or two-visit retreatment and, at 24 months, found equivalent healing (≈88%) between groups; critically, on multivariable analysis both lesion size and preoperative obturation length significantly affected outcome [[PMID:35488883]]. This is the closest paper in the evidence base to a prognostic-factor analysis for RCT outcomes, but cracks were not evaluated. The systematic reviews of vital pulp therapy (Cushley, Silva, Coll, Matoug-Elwerfelli, Fasoulas, Hatipoğlu) all address pulp capping and pulpotomy in carious or traumatic exposures, not RCT in cracked teeth, and are not applicable to this question [[PMID:33222178]] [[PMID:37254176]] [[PMID:35348216]] [[PMID:37710421]] [[PMID:40886932]]. The Zamparini et al. review of premixed bioceramic vs. epoxy resin sealers reported no significant differences in survival, success, or post-operative pain but likewise did not stratify by tooth condition [[PMID:38606520]].

**Level II — Prospective Studies**

None of the retrieved prospective studies evaluated cracked teeth. Zhang et al. reported a 90.4% one-year success for vital pulp therapy in pulpitic carious teeth using TheraCal LC and iRoot BP Plus, but the cohort did not include cracked teeth [[PMID:38701294]].

**Level IIIa–V**

No retrospective cohort, case-control, case series, or expert-opinion papers in the supplied evidence base addressed cracked-tooth prognosis after RCT by crack extent. This is a genuine gap in the retrieved literature for this question; the clinician should consult the dedicated cracked-tooth cohort literature (e.g., work by Krell, Rivera, Berman and others on cracked tooth outcomes stratified by crack depth and periodontal involvement) which was not returned in this search.

## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

The supplied evidence base does not directly address prognosis of endodontically treated cracked teeth stratified by crack extent — no included Cochrane review, systematic review, or trial in this retrieval evaluates cracked-tooth cohorts or crack-depth categories. What this evidence base does establish that bears on the case is that outcome of non-surgical root canal treatment tracks preoperative periapical lesion size and the technical quality of obturation [[PMID:35488883]], and that single-visit and two-visit protocols heal equivalently in single-rooted teeth with periapical lesions [[PMID:35488883]] [[PMID:27905673]] — both principles apply when planning endodontic treatment on a cracked tooth. Crack-extent-specific prognosis (crown-only vs. crown–root vs. crack extending to or below the crestal bone / pulpal floor) should be confirmed against the dedicated cracked-tooth cohort literature, which this search did not return; provisional guidance from outside this evidence base is that cracks confined to the crown with a vital or reversibly inflamed pulp carry the best prognosis, cracks extending subgingivally or to the pulpal floor carry a guarded-to-poor prognosis, and full-coverage cuspal protection immediately after RCT is standard of care.

Information that would change the recommendation: depth and direction of the crack on transillumination/CBCT/surgical exploration, presence and depth of an isolated periodontal probing defect, pulpal and periapical diagnosis, and whether the crack crosses the pulpal floor.

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The single Cochrane review retrieved (Manfredi et al., 2016; 25 RCTs, 3,780 participants) addresses single- vs multiple-visit root canal treatment generally and found no significant difference in radiological failure, tooth extraction, swelling, or sinus tract formation, though single-visit protocols carried a modestly higher rate of postoperative pain and analgesic use [[PMID:27905673]]. None of the included trials stratified outcomes by presence or extent of coronal cracking, so this review does not answer the clinical question directly; it only supports the general principle that visit protocol is not a major determinant of endodontic outcome — a principle that applies equally to cracked teeth.

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

No Level I evidence in this retrieval addresses cracked-tooth prognosis. The most relevant Level I signal comes from Karaoğlan et al. (2022), an RCT of 100 single-rooted teeth with periapical lesions undergoing retreatment, which identified preoperative lesion size and initial apical level of the root filling as the significant prognostic factors at 24 months — cracking was not analysed [[PMID:35488883]]. The remaining Level I evidence in this set addresses vital pulp therapy material choice (MTA/Biodentine vs calcium hydroxide) [[PMID:33222178]] [[PMID:37254176]] [[PMID:40886932]], bioceramic vs epoxy-resin sealers [[PMID:38606520]], and regenerative endodontics [[PMID:35579093]] — none evaluate cracked teeth as a distinct cohort or use crack extent as an outcome variable.

**Level II — Prospective Studies**

None retrieved that address cracked-tooth prognosis by crack extent. Zhang et al. (2024) prospectively evaluated vital pulp therapy in carious pulp exposures but did not stratify by cracking [[PMID:38701294]].

**Level IIIa / IIIb / IV / V**

No retrospective cohorts, case-control studies, case series, or expert-opinion documents in this evidence set address the outcome of RCT in cracked teeth stratified by crack extent. This is a notable gap: the dedicated cracked-tooth prognostic literature (e.g., AAE cracked-tooth cohort studies, Krell & Rivera, Kang et al., Tan et al., Sim et al.) was not returned by this retrieval and should be consulted separately before finalising prognosis and consent for the individual patient.
